Consider the following schema:

$$\begin{array} {l} \text{Sailors}(\; \underline{\textit{sid: } \textsf{integer}}, \textit{ sname: } \textsf{string}, \textit{ rating: } \textsf{integer}, \textit{ age: } \text{real}) \\ \text{Boats}(\; \underline{\textit{bid: } \textsf{integer}}, \textit{ bname: } \textsf{string}, \textit{ color: } \textsf{string)} \\ \text{Reserves}(\;\underline{\textit{sid: } \textsf{integer}, \textit{ bid: } \textsf{integer}, \textit{ day: } \textsf{date}}\;)\end{array} $$
The primary key fields are underlined, and the domain of each field is listed after the field name. Assume there are no NULL values in any column of any relation.

Consider the following query :

SELECT S.sname
FROM Sailors S, Reserves R, Boats B
WHERE S.sid = R.sid AND R.bid = B.bid
 AND (B.color = ‘blue’ AND B.color = ‘white’)

What is the output of the above query?

options.text: The names of sailors who have reserved a blue or a white boat.
The names of sailors who have reserved a blue AND a white boat.
The names of sailors who have reserved neither a blue nor a white boat.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 22)
The given query retrieves the names of sailors who have reserved a boat that is both blue and white. The integrity constraint that bid is a key for Boats tells us that the same boat cannot have two colors, and so this query will always return an empty answer set.
Source solution 2 (score: 7)
break down the query:

The query is selecting the names of sailors (S.sname) from the Sailors table (S), the Reserves table (R), and the Boats table (B).

The conditions in the where clause are:

1. S.sid = R.sid: This matches the sailor's ID with the reservation's sailor ID.
2. R.bid = B.bid: This matches the reservation's boat ID with the boat's ID.
3. (B.color = 'blue' AND B.color = 'white'): This is where the problem lies. This condition is trying to match boats that are both blue and white at the same time. However, a boat can only have one color, so this condition is impossible to satisfy.

Since the third condition is impossible to satisfy, the entire query will return an empty set. This is because the query is looking for sailors who have reserved boats that meet an impossible condition.

There4, the correct answer is: d .Empty set

--->In other words, the query will not return any names of sailors, because there are no boats that meet the impossible condition of being both blue and white at the same time.

Consider the following Student database and the relations in it :

$$\begin{array}{l} \textsf{Student (sid, name, marks)} \\ \textsf{Course (cid, min, max)} \end{array}$$
Student relation has the following set of tuples :
$$\{ ( 101, a, 50 ), (102, b, 52), (103, c, 60), (104, d, 70) \}$$
Course relation has the following set of tuples :
$$\{ (c1, 20, 90), (c2, 15, 95), (c3, 10, 100) \}$$
Consider the following query :

SELECT S.sid
FROM Student S
WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT COUNT(*)
 FROM Course C
 WHERE S.marks > C.min AND S.marks > C.max)


How many tuples will be in the output of the above SQL Query?
questions.solution:
Answer: 4

Source solution 1 (score: 79)
Note that for every tuple of Student relation, no tuple of Course relation satisfies the given condition, So, $\textsf{COUNT(*)}$ will give the output $0$ for every tuple of student relation. Hence, for every tuple of student relation, the $\textsf{EXISTS}$ will return TRUE. So, four rows will be printed.

$\textsf{EXISTS}$ return false if its input is Empty Set.

In the given query, input to $\textsf{EXISTS}$ is $\textsf{COUNT(*)}$ which returns an integer value $\geq 0,$ but never Empty Set.

So, $\textsf{EXISTS}$ always returns TRUE here and we get $4$ rows in the output.
Source solution 2 (score: 7)
      • Comparisons:
        • c1: 50 > 20 (True) AND 50 > 90 (False) → No match
        • c2: 50 > 15 (True) AND 50 > 95 (False) → No match
        • c3: 50 > 10 (True) AND 50 > 100 (False) → No match
      • Subquery returns 0 rows → EXISTS = False.
  • Comparisons:
    • c1: 52 > 20 (True) AND 52 > 90 (False) → No match
    • c2: 52 > 15 (True) AND 52 > 95 (False) → No match
    • c3: 52 > 10 (True) AND 52 > 100 (False) → No match
  • Subquery returns 0 rows → EXISTS = False.
  • Comparisons:
    • c1: 60 > 20 (True) AND 60 > 90 (False) → No match
    • c2: 60 > 15 (True) AND 60 > 95 (False) → No match
    • c3: 60 > 10 (True) AND 60 > 100 (False) → No match
  • Subquery returns 0 rows → EXISTS = False.
  • Comparisons:
    • c1: 70 > 20 (True) AND 70 > 90 (False) → No match
    • c2: 70 > 15 (True) AND 70 > 95 (False) → No match
    • c3: 70 > 10 (True) AND 70 > 100 (False) → No match
  • Subquery returns 0 rows → EXISTS = False.
  • When you use COUNT(*) inside an EXISTS subquery, it behaves slightly differently than when you use COUNT(*) in a regular SELECT query. The key point is that the EXISTS operator doesn't actually care about the value returned by COUNT(*). It simply checks if the subquery produces any rows, regardless of whether those rows are empty or contain data.

  • The EXISTS clause: This checks whether the subquery returns any rows. It will return TRUE if the subquery produces one or more rows and FALSE if the subquery produces no rows at all.

  • COUNT(*) in the subquery: The COUNT(*) will count how many rows satisfy the condition. Even if it counts 0 rows, the subquery still executes and produces one row (with the value 0 in this case). The result of COUNT(*) is irrelevant for the EXISTS condition.

    • The subquery itself still exists and produces one result (even if that result is 0).
    • EXISTS only cares whether the subquery returned a result, not the value of the result. As long as the subquery produces at least one row (in this case, the 0 value), the EXISTS condition will evaluate as TRUE.
Source solution 3 (score: 3)

Answer 4

Observe the subquerry condition in the question , (S.marks>C.min AND S.marks>C.max) this returns "Nothing" since there is no such tuple that satisfying the condition.

So, we have NOTHING as an input in the count(*) finally gives the value of the whole Subquerry as "zero".

Now coming to the main query we have EXISTS which return false iff it has emptyset as the input. Since zero is cannot be an empty set the main query will return all the 4 tuples in the Student table.

Therefore answer is 4.

questions.qtext: Given relations $r$ and $s$. Let Function $\text{C}$ denote the number of results in the output. Which of the following statements "can be" correct? (Hint: Discard the statements which are NEVER possible)
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 15)
Left and right outer joins can yield result set of sizes both greater or smaller than each other depending on the data. Full outerjoin will always have a set size greater than (or equal to) the result of left or right joins.
Source solution 2 (score: 3)

" CAN BE "
so option D.

Source solution 3 (score: 2)

To solve this problem, we need to compare the cardinalities (number of results) of different types of relational algebra joins. Let's define the symbols first:

  • $r \bowtie s$ : Inner Join (Returns only matching rows from both relations).

  • $r \ltimes s$ : Left Outer Join (Returns all rows from $r$, plus matching rows from $s$. Unmatched rows from $r$ are padded with NULLs).

  • $r \rtimes s$ : Right Outer Join (Returns all rows from $s$, plus matching rows from $r$. Unmatched rows from $s$ are padded with NULLs).

  • $r \bowtie s$ : Full Outer Join (Returns all rows from both $r$ and $s$, padding with NULLs where there is no match).

Analyzing the Statements

The core rule for these joins is that an Inner Join is a subset of an Outer Join. Therefore, the cardinality of an Outer Join will always be greater than or equal to the cardinality of an Inner Join.

I. $C(r \bowtie s) > C(r \ltimes s)$

  • Analysis: This statement says the Inner Join has more results than the Left Outer Join.

  • Status: Impossible. The Left Outer Join contains every row that the Inner Join does, plus any non-matching rows from $r$. Thus, $C(r \ltimes s) \geq C(r \bowtie s)$ always.

II. $C(r \ltimes s) > C(r \bowtie s)$

  • Analysis: This says the Left Outer Join has more results than the Full Outer Join.

  • Status: Impossible. The Full Outer Join contains all rows from the Left Outer Join, plus any non-matching rows from $s$. Thus, $C(r \bowtie s) \geq C(r \ltimes s)$ always.

III. $C(r \bowtie s) > C(r \bowtie s)$

  • Analysis: This says the Full Outer Join has more results than the Inner Join.

  • Status: Possible. This is true whenever there is at least one row in $r$ or $s$ that does not have a match in the other relation.

IV. $C(r \ltimes s) > C(r \rtimes s)$

  • Analysis: This says the Left Outer Join has more results than the Right Outer Join.

  • Status: Possible. This occurs if the number of non-matching rows in $r$ is greater than the number of non-matching rows in $s$. For example, if $r$ has 10 unmatched rows and $s$ has 2, the Left Outer Join will be larger.

Conclusion

Statements III and IV "can be" correct depending on the data in the relations. Statements I and II violate the fundamental definitions of these relational operations.

Correct Answer: D. III and IV

Let $\mathrm{R}(a, b, c, d)$ be a RDBMS relation having the following set of functional dependencies(FD set) :
FD Set $\mathrm{F}=\{b \rightarrow c ; c \rightarrow d ; ab \rightarrow d ; bc \rightarrow cd\}$ We apply some queries on a relational instance $r$ of $\text{R}$. Which of the following queries are guaranteed to return the same number of tuples as in relation instance $r?$
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 23)
From the given FD set we can find candidate key which is “$ab$” because these attributes do not appear on the RHS of any FD.

The number of tuples in a relation resulting from a PROJECT operation is always less than or equal to the number of tuples in $\text{R}.$

If the projection list is a superkey of $\text{R}$—that is, it includes some key of $\text{R}$— the resulting relation has the same number of tuples as $\text{R}.$
Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Answer option C,D

Since, AB is the candidate key because we can infer any other attributes in relation R using FD set.

For the queries in the options to return the same no of tuples as in the relation R we need AB under Projection(π) operation, since AB is the key. So option C is correct.

Now, Any SUPERSET of the attributes AB(candidate key) will definitely give the same result as AB(candidate key) under Projection (π) operation. From this we can say option d gives same result as option c

Therefore OPTION C D are correct

For a RDBMS relation $\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}, \mathrm{R}, \mathrm{S}, \mathrm{U})$, the following set $\mathrm{F}$ of functional dependencies holds:
$$
\mathrm{F}=\{\mathrm{P} \rightarrow \mathrm{QR} ; \mathrm{RS} \rightarrow \mathrm{U} ; \mathrm{Q} \rightarrow \mathrm{S} ; \mathrm{U} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}\}
$$

  • Ram decomposes $\mathrm{T}$ into two relations $\mathrm{X}(\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}, \mathrm{R}), \mathrm{Y}(\mathrm{R}, \mathrm{S}, \mathrm{U})$.
  • Shyam decomposes $\mathrm{T}$ into two relations $\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}, \mathrm{R}), \mathrm{B}(\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{S}, \mathrm{U})$.

Which of the following is/are necessarily true on any(every) instance $t$ of relation $\mathrm{T}?$
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 25)

$\text{T(PQRSU)} :$
$\mathrm{F}=\{\mathrm{P} \rightarrow \mathrm{QR} ; \mathrm{RS} \rightarrow \mathrm{U} ; \mathrm{Q} \rightarrow \mathrm{S} ; \mathrm{U} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}\}$
The candidate keys are : $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{U}, \mathrm{RS}, \mathrm{QR}$
A decomposition $\{R 1, R 2\}$ is a lossless-join decomposition if $\mathrm{R} 1 \cap \mathrm{R} 2 \rightarrow$
$\mathrm{R} 1$ or $\mathrm{R} 1 \cap \mathrm{R} 2 \rightarrow \mathrm{R} 2$.
Since Shyam's decomposition $: \text{A(P, Q, R) , B(P,S,U)}.$
and $\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B}=\mathrm{P}$. Since $\mathrm{P}$ is a candidate key, Therefore $\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}$.
So lossless decomposition. Hence, $\text{A} \bowtie \text{B}=t$.
Ram's decomposition is NOT lossless because common attribute $\mathrm{R}$ is Not super key in either $\mathrm{X}$ or $\mathrm{Y}$. So, $\mathrm{X} \bowtie \mathrm{Y}$ may or may not be equal to $t$.
